clinicalPearls: A clonal disorder with overlapping myelodysplastic and myeloproliferative features, defined by persistent peripheral blood monocytosis
It occurs mainly in older adults and presents with cytopenias, monocytosis, splenomegaly or constitutional symptoms
Diagnosis requires sustained monocytosis with monocytes forming a significant fraction of the white cells, and exclusion of other causes
The BCR-ABL1 fusion must be absent, distinguishing it from chronic myeloid leukaemia
Common mutations include TET2, SRSF2 and ASXL1, and prognostic scores guide management
It carries a risk of progression to acute myeloid leukaemia
reference.pathophysiology: Chronic myelomonocytic leukaemia is a clonal haematopoietic stem cell neoplasm with both dysplastic (ineffective haematopoiesis causing cytopenias) and proliferative (monocytosis, sometimes leucocytosis and organomegaly) features. Recurrent mutations in epigenetic regulators and splicing genes such as TET2, SRSF2 and ASXL1 drive the clonal expansion and the characteristic monocyte proliferation. Ineffective and dysplastic maturation produces the peripheral cytopenias, and accumulation of blasts over time can culminate in transformation to acute myeloid leukaemia.
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and film confirming sustained monocytosis
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine with cytogenetics
BCR-ABL1 testing to exclude chronic myeloid leukaemia
Molecular panel (for example TET2, SRSF2, ASXL1)
Assessment for reactive causes of monocytosis
redFlags: Rising blast count indicating progression to acute leukaemia
Worsening cytopenias with bleeding or infection
Rapidly enlarging spleen or proliferative features
reference.prognosis: The course is heterogeneous; prognosis depends on blast percentage, cytogenetics, mutations and blood counts, ranging from indolent disease to rapid progression to acute myeloid leukaemia.
pitfalls: Attributing persistent monocytosis to a reactive cause without excluding CMML
Not testing for BCR-ABL1 to exclude chronic myeloid leukaemia
Underusing prognostic scoring to guide therapy
management: Risk-adapted management using prognostic scoring, with hypomethylating agents (azacitidine or decitabine) for higher-risk or dysplastic disease
Allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation as the only curative option for eligible higher-risk patients
Cytoreduction with hydroxycarbamide to control the proliferative phenotype, symptomatic leucocytosis and splenomegaly
Supportive care with red-cell transfusion and erythropoiesis-stimulating agents for anaemia, and prompt treatment of infection during cytopenias
Serial monitoring of blood counts and marrow blast percentage for disease progression
Surveillance for transformation to acute myeloid leukaemia
Haematology-led multidisciplinary care with consideration of clinical trials
